endings.text: End of the walk. They waited less than a year. In 1905 they married in London, at St. Margaret's, Westminster; the licence gave Delia as 46 and Field as 70. "The ceremony was quiet, and attended only by a few friends." They came home to Chicago as man and wife, and in January 1906 Marshall Field was dead of pneumonia, caught on a New Year's golf course with Robert Todd Lincoln. After thirty years of waiting they had a few months. Delia got $1 million and the house, moved to Washington, where her mansion was called the Pink Palace, and lived until 1937.

evidence.text: Arthur J. Caton died 'November 18, 1904, at New York's Waldorf-Astoria hotel'. 'The cause of death was inexact. Some said he succumbed to liver failure. Others ascribed the demise to peritonitis.' An Ottawa, Illinois Times story suggested he may have taken his own life.

evidence.locator: Other Mrs. Field: the paragraphs on Delia and the Catons; Second Mrs. Field: 'Delia Spencer married Arthur Caton in 1876.'
evidence.text: Delia Spencer, the daughter of one of the founders of the Hibbard, Spencer & Bartlett hardware firm, married Arthur Caton in 1876. He was the son of Judge John Dean Caton, one of Illinois' first chief justices; a lawyer, sportsman and clubman, he loved golf and polo and bred horses and dogs on the family's Ottawa farm.

evidence.locator: The paragraph quoting Meeker on the Catons' entertaining.
evidence.text: Arthur Meeker's mother 'always declared that nobody ever gave such wonderful parties as Delia Caton'. The Catons had no children and entertained in 'their big, elaborate house on Calumet Avenue'.

The Merchant and Mrs. Caton: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Merchant and Mrs. Caton: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

evidence.locator: Second Mrs. Field: the Meeker paragraph; Other Mrs. Field: the Beveridge Chronicle's 'subterranean tunnel'.
evidence.text: Arthur Meeker: 'The gossip of the day cast the worst light on the affair; it was even absurdly asserted that an underground tunnel connected the Caton house on Calumet with the Field house on Prairie, which was just in front of it, or just back.'

evidence.locator: The paragraph quoting The Chronicle of Catherine Eddy Beveridge.
evidence.text: There were rumours that Field and Delia Caton were lovers for nearly 30 years, and 'Delia sometimes traveled to Europe with Marshall Field without Arthur accompanying them.'

evidence.locator: The post's opening paragraphs and the paragraph on Nannie's death.
evidence.text: Field proposed to Nannie Douglas Scott by jumping aboard her train as it left Chicago; he got off at the next stop and walked back to work. Their marriage foundered: by Longstreet's account 'Mrs. Field led Marshall Field a hell-on-earth life'. Nannie took to the South of France, and died in France in 1896.

The census of 1 June 1900 enumerated John Dunford, coachman, born in England, as the head of his own household in the rear building behind 1905 Prairie, and Thomas Benson, butler, born in Ireland, in the house.

Marshall and Nannie Field had three children: Louis, who died in infancy, and Marshall, Jr. and Ethel, raised at 1905 Prairie, 'the first in Chicago to be completely wired for electricity', built in 1876 at a cost of some $2 million.

Meeker: 'he fell in love with his friend's wife years before he was able to marry her.' And: 'In the Nineties, divorce was unthinkable: they had to wait for him (Arthur Caton) to die, which, distressingly, he didn't do until 1904.'
Marshall Field Residence, 1905 S. Prairie Avenue: later converted to an aeronautical university. Razed 1955.

evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on the store, his wealth, his son and his death.
evidence.text: Marshall Field: 'Give the lady what she wants'; 'the wealthiest and most powerful businessman in Chicago', his fortune valued at $125 million in 1905. His son Marshall Field Jr. was shot on 22 November 1905; Field himself died of pneumonia on 16 January 1906, caught after a New Year's Day golf game with, among others, Robert Todd Lincoln.

evidence.locator: The paragraph quoting Meeker, Chicago, With Love.
evidence.text: Field was reluctant to make a speech at one of the Catons' grand dinners, and Delia sprang to her feet and said: Mr. Field just wants me to remind you that the White Sale starts next Monday.

evidence.locator: Second Mrs. Field: the paragraphs on the marriage and after; Wikipedia: the death on 16 January 1906.
evidence.text: The marriage licence acquired in London in 1905 gave Delia as 46 and Field as 70. They married at St. Margaret's, Westminster; 'The ceremony was quiet, and attended only by a few friends.' Field died in 1906 of pneumonia after a round of golf in a foursome that included Robert Todd Lincoln. Delia was left $1 million and the Field mansion on Prairie Avenue, moved to Washington, D.C., where her house was known as the Pink Palace, and died in 1937.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE MERCHANT AND MRS. CATON. Monday morning, 21 November 1904. A telegram has come from New York, and the blinds are down in a house on Calumet Avenue.

Four stops, on foot, from the widow's door, through the back yards the servants share, to the front steps of Marshall Field, the merchant prince of Chicago. Everybody on Prairie Avenue knows this story. Nobody says it out loud. Thirty years of dinners, voyages and rumours are about to come to an end, and this morning the only people talking are the ones who carry the coal.

Start at Calumet Avenue, at the house with the drawn blinds.

armour_corwith_house_1945_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Henry Corwith here. Before them, the Armour household lived here (1890-1891).

armour_house_2115_prairie.text: A stone house with a steep mansard roof, built for the lumberman David Kelley. The family of the meatpacker Philip D. Armour lived here for nearly 50 years. Armour's widow was one of the last people living on the street.

buckingham_house_2036_prairie.text: Clarence Buckingham's house in the 1904 Blue Book. In 1927 his sister Kate will give Chicago the Buckingham Fountain in his memory, its centre jet throwing water 150 feet up.

coleman_ames_house_1811_prairie.text: A Romanesque house of rough brown sandstone, built in 1886 for Joseph G. Coleman. Cobb and Frost were the architects. It still stands.

dent_house_1823_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Thomas Dent here, a lawyer by the 1900 census.

dexter_house_1721_prairie.text: Wirt Dexter's house of 1863, given a new front by Arthur Little in 1889. By 1904 the Blue Book lists Henry H. Walker here.

dexter_house_1721_prairie_frame_house.text: Wirt Dexter's frame house of 1863, the first house on this lot. Arthur Little's brick front on Prairie Avenue was built onto its street end; the old house's own front, porch and bay windows, faces the side yard.

edson_keith_house_1906_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Edson Keith here.

elbridge_keith_house_1900_prairie.text: A limestone house with a steep slate roof, built for Elbridge Keith, a hat merchant who became a banker. The top floor inside that roof was added in the 1880s. It is the last Second Empire house left on Prairie Avenue.

fort_dearborn_massacre_monument_1893.text: A bronze group by Carl Rohl-Smith, paid for by George M. Pullman and set up beside his house in 1893. It shows the Potawatomi leader Black Partridge saving Margaret Helm during the battle of August 1812.

george_glessner_house_1706_prairie.text: Home of George M. Glessner, son of the granite house at 1800; the Glessners built it beside his sister's house at 1700.

glessner_house.text: A granite fortress on the street, with a sunny courtyard inside. People passing by remarked on its narrow windows along 18th Street, not knowing the big ones face the courtyard. By 1904 John and Frances Glessner had lived here since 1887.

glessner_lee_house_1700_prairie.text: Built by the Glessners for their daughter Frances, who married Blewett Lee in 1898. Decades on she will build the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, tiny crime scenes still used to train investigators.

goodman_house_1612_prairie.text: Joseph Goodman's stone Italianate of 1869, two years before the Great Fire: round-headed windows under long keystones, and an arched portico at the top of a high stoop.

henderson_house_1816_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Charles M. Henderson here. Before them, W. H. Merrill jr. lived here (1899-1903).

hibbard_house_1701_prairie.text: William G. Hibbard's house of 1869, by William Le Baron Jenney, who fifteen years later built the Home Insurance Building, called the first skyscraper.

law_house_1620_prairie.text: Robert Law's house, engraved in 1874 for a series on the homes of Chicago: two storeys over a raised basement under a slated mansard.

marsh_house_1824_prairie.text: Samuel B. Pomeroy's Italianate villa of 1857, one of the oldest houses on the street, hiding behind the stone front George B. Marsh gave it after 1880.

marshall_field_house_1905_prairie.text: Marshall Field's house, by Richard Morris Hunt, the architect of the Statue of Liberty's pedestal. Field is the wealthiest businessman in Chicago, and the street's most famous neighbour.

marshall_field_jr_house_1919_prairie.text: Built in 1867 and made bigger several times. Marshall Field Jr. bought it in 1890. In 1902 D. H. Burnham and Company added a huge new part.

moulton_lowden_house_1912_prairie.text: A big house in the French château style, built in 1882 for B. P. Moulton. In 1898 Frank O. Lowden moved in. He later became governor of Illinois.

premise: Three days after Arthur Caton died in a New York hotel, the whole street is whispering about his widow Delia and the richest man in Chicago, whose house stands just across the alley.

stage.caption: A maid opens the Caton door to an early caller, and the coachman waits at the curb with his hat in his hand.

The Caton coachman (no card in the town; an unnamed figure)

stops.text: Calumet Avenue, behind Prairie. This is the Caton house, and its blinds are drawn. On Friday Arthur J. Caton died at New York's Waldorf-Astoria hotel, and nobody can quite say of what. "Some said he succumbed to liver failure. Others ascribed the demise to peritonitis." A newspaper downstate will hint that he took his own life. He was a judge's son, a lawyer who loved golf and polo and bred horses and dogs on the family farm. His wife Delia, a hardware heiress he married in 1876, gave the best parties in town: Arthur Meeker's mother "always declared that nobody ever gave such wonderful parties as Delia Caton". There were no children. This morning there is a widow, a house full of servants, and a caller on the steps. Go round the back, to the yards between Calumet and Prairie.

stage.caption: Karolina Hall comes over from the Field yard to the fence, where a Caton maid is waiting with the news.

cast.name: A Caton laundress (no card in the town; an unnamed figure)

stops.text: The back yards, where Calumet meets Prairie at the rear fence. Turn round and the Field house is right there, its coach house on the alley. The servants of the two houses have shared this ground for years, and they have heard the talk. Arthur Meeker, who grew up on this street, wrote it down: "it was even absurdly asserted that an underground tunnel connected the Caton house on Calumet with the Field house on Prairie, which was just in front of it, or just back." Meeker called it absurd, and it was. But a society diarist recorded that "Delia sometimes traveled to Europe with Marshall Field without Arthur accompanying them." Now Arthur is dead, Field's wife has been dead eight years, and a laundress from the Field house is leaning on the fence. Walk on to Prairie Avenue and find the man himself.

stage.caption: Marshall Field comes out of his door, and stops on the steps to look east, toward Calumet Avenue, before his coachman reaches him.

stops.text: 1905 Prairie, the Marshall Field house: built in 1876 for some $2 million, "the first in Chicago to be completely wired for electricity". Field is the richest merchant in the city. Years ago he proposed to his first wife by jumping aboard her train as it left Chicago; one account says that "Mrs. Field led Marshall Field a hell-on-earth life", and Nannie Field died in France in 1896. Meeker put the rest plainly: "he fell in love with his friend's wife years before he was able to marry her." And: "In the Nineties, divorce was unthinkable: they had to wait for him (Arthur Caton) to die, which, distressingly, he didn't do until 1904." That was Friday. Thomas Benson, the butler, has the door; John Dunford, the coachman, comes round from the stable. The house will be razed in 1955.

stage.caption: Two ladies of the street walk past the Field house with their heads together, and do not look at it.

cast.name: A second lady of the street (unnamed)

stops.text: From up the street the Field house looks like any other on the row. It is not. Field never liked making speeches, and one night at one of the Catons' grand dinners he was called on to say a few words. Delia sprang to her feet and spoke for him: "Mr. Field just wants me to remind you that the White Sale starts next Monday." It was a joke about his store, made by another man's wife, at her husband's table, and the guests who told it afterwards told it as the night everybody saw how close those two were. The ladies passing the Field house this morning are not looking at it, and they are talking about nothing else. Arthur Caton is not yet buried. Everyone can guess what happens next, and nobody can say it.

title: The Merchant and Mrs. Caton
